transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, yeah, thanks. So, I'm mostly here because I’ve started planning my whole day around, well, not using elevators. It’s getting a bit out of hand. Like, I’m taking five flights of stairs at my apartment every single day. Which, honestly, my calves are getting pretty strong from it, and I used to run track in high school so I don't mind the exercise, but it's exhausting when I'm carrying groceries, you know? 

But the real issue is how it's messing with my job. I'm a training specialist, I do a lot of tech and development stuff, and I actually just had to turn down leading this really cool workshop just because it was in a high-rise. The workshop was on this new scheduling software that I actually helped beta test, which was a huge deal for me because I mostly taught myself everything after I graduated, but I just couldn't do the building. 

And... I even had to stop doing house visits with one of my older computer students. His name is Arthur, really nice guy, he's just trying to learn how to video call his grandkids out in Arizona. I've never been to Arizona, but I hear the heat is a dry heat, so maybe it's not too bad compared to here? But anyway, Arthur's building doesn’t really have another option besides the elevator, like the stairs are locked or something, so I just had to stop seeing him. I just can't do the elevator thing, and it's starting to get in the way.
What is it about elevators that makes you want to avoid them?

Well, it's... I mean, I know an elevator in an office block is probably safe, right? Like, they have to pass inspections and stuff. I actually read this article once about elevator inspectors, and it's wild how much they have to check. They look at the cables and the brakes—which, apparently, modern elevators have these crazy safety brakes that make it almost impossible for them to free-fall. 

But, like, when I look at those old doors in my apartment building, or even the ones at work, my mind just... it treats it like I’m about to get trapped in there. Or dropped. Even though part of me knows that sounds completely over the top, especially after reading about the brakes. It's just this overwhelming feeling. Kind of like when I tried to ride that drop tower at the state fair a few years ago. Have you ever been to the state fair? The fried Oreos are amazing, but that ride was a huge mistake. I thought I was going to die. I guess looking at an elevator gives me that exact same feeling, even if I'm just standing in the lobby holding a bag of groceries.
Do you experience a similar feeling when you're in other small or enclosed spaces, like a car in heavy traffic or a small room?

No, not at all. Small rooms are totally fine, and cars... cars are actually kind of my safe space. I love driving. I have this older Honda Civic, and I actually just put a new sound system in it myself last month. Taking apart the dashboard was super tedious, honestly, because those little plastic clips always snap if you aren't careful. I had to watch, like, four different YouTube tutorials just to figure out the wiring harness. 

The guy in one of the videos had this amazing garage setup, with all these neon signs and a massive pegboard for his tools. I’d love to have a garage like that someday, but my apartment complex barely even has enough parking spots as it is. People are always leaving passive-aggressive notes on windshields if you park even an inch over the line, which is super annoying, especially when it's raining and you're just trying to run inside. But, uh... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, enclosed spaces. Yeah, sitting in heavy traffic in my car doesn't bother me one bit. It's really just the elevators.
Do you experience a similar feeling when you're in high places, like near a ledge or at the top of a tall building?

No, high places don't really bother me. I mean, as long as I don't have to take an elevator to get up there, right? I actually went hiking up in the mountains a couple of years ago with some friends. We drove out to this trail—my buddy drove his Jeep, which was cool, but man, the suspension on those things is so stiff, I felt every single rock on the dirt road. We ended up at this overlook that was crazy high up, just a sheer drop-off. And I felt totally fine standing near the edge. 

We actually brought a picnic up there. Sandwiches from this little deli near my place. They make this incredible spicy Italian sub, like, they use this special pepper relish that just makes the whole thing. I've tried to recreate it at home, but I can never get the vinegar ratio right. I think they might use some sort of artisan balsamic or something. But yeah, standing up there, looking out over the whole valley while eating that sandwich... it was great. No panic at all. So, no, it's definitely not a height thing.
What exactly do you think might happen if you were to get trapped in an elevator?

I don't know, honestly. I guess I just picture the doors getting stuck and me just... being stuck in there forever. Or until the air runs out. Which I know doesn't actually happen, they aren't airtight. I saw this documentary once about how buildings are ventilated, and it's actually super fascinating. They have all these massive ducts and fans up on the roof, and the system is designed to keep the air pressure balanced throughout the whole building. 

The guy in the documentary was explaining how they have to clean those ducts, and it looked like the worst job ever. They send these little remote-controlled robots with cameras and brushes on them down into the vents. I actually looked up how much those robots cost because I thought it would be a cool toy to mess around with, maybe attach a camera to it and see what my cat does when it chases him around the apartment. My cat, Barnaby, he's a trip. He's this orange tabby, and he has this weird obsession with knocking my pens off the desk. Every single time I sit down to work, swat, swat, there goes the pen. I had to buy a special heavy-duty pen holder just to keep him out of it. 

But, um... yeah, getting trapped. I just... I don't really know what would happen, but the thought of it just makes my chest tight.
Is it the thought of being in a small, enclosed space like an elevator that scares you, or is it something more specific about elevators themselves?

I think it's just elevators specifically. Like, I know an elevator in a nice, modern office block is probably completely safe, right? But when I look at those old, clunky doors in my apartment building, or even the ones at my work, my mind just immediately goes to this place where I'm convinced I'm about to get trapped in there, or the cables are going to snap and drop me. Even though part of me knows that sounds totally over the top and dramatic. 

Actually, the elevator at my work is the absolute worst. I work as a training specialist for this corporate tech company, and our building is from, like, the 1970s. The carpet in the hallways is this hideous orange and brown geometric pattern. It honestly looks like something out of a bad sci-fi movie. I was actually talking to the facilities manager about it last week—nice guy, his name is Dave, always wears these really loud Hawaiian shirts. He was telling me that they're finally going to renovate the whole floor next spring. They're going to put in hardwood, or well, that fake laminate stuff that looks like hardwood, which is probably easier to clean anyway. I spilled coffee on that orange carpet on my second day of work, and let me tell you, getting a stain out of 40-year-old carpet is impossible. I tried club soda, dish soap, everything. I ended up just having to put a potted plant over the spot so my boss wouldn't see it. It's a snake plant, actually, because I read they're impossible to kill, and I have a terrible track record with plants. 

But yeah... what was I saying? Oh, right. The old doors. Yeah, looking at those old elevator doors just makes my brain think I'm going to get stuck or dropped, even if I know it's probably fine.
Do you think your fear of elevators is because you feel like you're not in control when you're inside one?

I mean, maybe? I haven't really thought about it like that. Control is a weird thing, you know? Like, I guess I don't have control in an elevator, but I also don't have control when I'm flying, or even just sitting in the passenger seat of a car. 

My buddy Mike, the one with the Jeep I mentioned earlier, he is the absolute worst driver. He treats the gas pedal like it's an on-off switch. We were driving down to the city last weekend to go to this vintage arcade bar—they have all these classic pinball machines, which are so hard to find in good working condition nowadays. I spent like twenty bucks just playing the Addams Family pinball machine. The flippers on it were perfectly calibrated, it was awesome. But anyway, Mike was driving us down there, and we got stuck in this massive traffic jam on the interstate. Just bumper to bumper for miles because of some construction. I had zero control over the situation, just sitting there in the passenger seat listening to him complain about the brake lights in front of us. 

He was listening to this podcast about deep-sea diving, which honestly sounded terrifying. Just being down in the pitch black with all that water pressure, and these weird glowing fish... I don't know how people do that for a living. But I didn't feel panicky in the car at all, you know? Just annoyed that we were going to be late for the arcade. So... yeah, I don't really know if it's a control thing with the elevators. I just really, really don't want to get in them.
Do you think you would feel less anxious about elevators if you were in control of the elevator, for example, if you were the one operating it?

I don't know, maybe? If I had like a joystick or something and I could steer it? But elevators don't really work like that, do they? You just push a button and hope for the best. It's not like driving a forklift. 

Actually, I had to get certified to drive a forklift at my first job out of high school. It was this massive warehouse that distributed pet supplies. Dog food, cat litter, those giant scratching posts... you wouldn't believe how heavy a pallet of clumping cat litter is. I had to take this two-day training course, and the instructor was this old guy named Earl who chewed on unlit cigars the entire time. Never lit them, just chewed on them. He was super strict about the speed limit in the warehouse, which was like five miles an hour. It felt like you were crawling. But honestly, driving that forklift was kind of fun once I got the hang of it. You use these levers to tilt the forks and lift the pallets, and the steering is in the back wheels, so it turns really sharp. I got pretty good at whipping it around the corners of the aisles, avoiding the giant stacks of rawhide bones. 

But yeah, an elevator... I don't think they even have manual controls anymore, do they? Unless you're like a firefighter with a special key. So I'm not really sure if it would help. I just know I don't like getting in them.
Would you feel less anxious if you were accompanied by someone you trust when taking the elevator?

I mean, I don't really know if having someone with me would make a difference. Maybe? But honestly, I usually just take the stairs anyway, even when I'm with other people. 

Like, the other day I was getting lunch with my coworker, Sarah. We were going to this new deli that opened up down the street from our office. They have these amazing pastrami sandwiches—like, the meat is stacked so high you can barely get your mouth around it. And they make their own pickles in-house, which are super crunchy and garlicky. Anyway, Sarah is one of those people who always wears heels, even though our office is pretty casual. She has this massive collection of them under her desk. She was complaining about her feet hurting and wanted to take the elevator down from the fourth floor, and I just told her I'd meet her in the lobby. I just took the stairs. 

I've gotten pretty fast at taking the stairs, actually. I try to skip every other step on the way down, it kind of feels like a workout. I used to run cross-country in high school, so I guess I still have some of that stamina. We had this coach, Coach Miller, who would make us run hills in the pouring rain. He used to say it built character, but I think he just liked watching us suffer. 

But yeah, I don't know if having someone with me in the elevator would help. I haven't really tried it lately because I just avoid them altogether.
Do you feel anxious or uncomfortable in other situations where you have no control?

I don't really think so? Like I said about the car ride with Mike, I didn't feel panicky or anything just sitting there in traffic. Or like... airplanes, you know? I'm totally fine flying. 

Actually, I flew out to Denver last year for my cousin's wedding. It was this gorgeous outdoor ceremony up in the mountains. The air up there is so thin, though, it totally messes with you. I tried to go for a run the first morning and I was winded after like half a mile. But the flight itself was totally fine. I had a window seat, which I always try to get because I like leaning my head against the wall to sleep. The guy next to me, though, he kept falling asleep and leaning onto my shoulder. He was wearing this really strong cologne, kind of smelled like pine needles and cheap aftershave. I didn't want to wake him up because he looked exhausted, but it was super awkward. They served these tiny little bags of pretzels, and I swear they put extra salt on them so you buy more drinks. 

But yeah, on the plane, I'm literally thousands of feet in the air in a metal tube, totally not in control of anything, and I'm fine. It's really just the elevators that freak me out. I don't know why.
Do you think your fear of elevators would decrease if you knew someone was constantly monitoring the elevator's systems and could intervene if something went wrong?

I don't really know if that would help, honestly. Knowing someone is watching... I mean, who is watching? Is it just some guy in a basement somewhere? 

Because my buddy Greg used to work security for this big office building downtown, and his whole job was basically just watching camera feeds. He said it was the most boring job in the world. He'd sit in this little room with no windows, staring at like twenty different screens for eight hours a day. He used to bring his Nintendo Switch and just play Zelda under the desk the whole time. He told me he once watched a guy spend twenty minutes trying to figure out how to use the revolving door before he realized he had to push it. Greg didn't even go help him, he just sat there laughing. He eventually got fired because he fell asleep on a night shift and someone stole a bunch of laptops from the third floor. 

So yeah, if someone like Greg is the one monitoring the elevator, I definitely don't think that would make me feel any better. I just... I don't know, it's just the elevator itself, you know? I don't think knowing someone is watching the systems would change how I feel about getting inside one.
Do you think you would be afraid of elevators if you were the one operating the controls?

Operating the controls? Like... being an elevator operator? I honestly have no idea. Do they even have those anymore? I guess I've seen them in old movies. But if I was the one pressing the buttons and driving it... maybe? But it's still just a box hanging by a wire, you know? 

Speaking of operating stuff, though, at my job—I do training and development—we just had to roll out this massive new training module for the forklift drivers at our main warehouse. Have you ever driven a forklift? They're actually wild because they steer from the back wheels instead of the front, so it totally messes with your head when you first try to turn. We had this one guy, total rookie, he was doing his practical exam last week and he completely misjudged the turning radius. He backed right into a pallet of those huge, industrial-sized tubs of mayonnaise. It was a complete disaster. It literally looked like a bomb went off, just white goop all over the concrete floor, all over the forklift tires, all over his boots. We had to shut down that whole loading dock for like three hours just to mop it up. The smell was awful, too, kind of like vinegar and old eggs. We ended up having to rewrite a whole section of the safety manual just because of that guy. 

But anyway... what was the question? Oh, elevator controls. Yeah, I don't know if me driving it would really change anything. I think I'd still just rather take the stairs.
Would your fear of elevators decrease if you had a way to exit the elevator quickly in case of an emergency?

Exit quickly? Like... if there was an emergency hatch or something? I mean, I guess maybe that would help a little bit? If I knew I could just pop the roof open and climb out. But honestly, I don't know how I'd even reach the ceiling. 

Actually, that reminds me of this escape room I did for my friend Sarah's birthday last month. Have you ever done one of those? We did this one that was themed like a 1920s speakeasy, and we had an hour to find the mob boss's ledger before the cops showed up. It was so intense. We got completely stuck on this one puzzle with a grandfather clock where you had to set the hands to a specific time based on a riddle hidden in a painting. We wasted like twenty minutes on it because Sarah's boyfriend, Dave, insisted he knew how to solve it without using any of our hints. Dave is one of those guys who always has to be right, you know? He works in finance and he talks about crypto literally non-stop. Anyway, he completely botched the clock puzzle, and we ended up failing the room. The game master had to come in and unlock the door for us, which was super embarrassing. But the crazy part was, the final key was actually hidden inside a fake bottle of whiskey on the bar the whole time. We didn't even think to check it. We all went out for tacos after, though, so it wasn't a total loss. I had these amazing al pastor tacos with pineapple. 

But yeah, I don't know if having a quick exit in an elevator would really fix it for me. I think I'd still just be panicking the whole time I was trying to get out.
Do you think your fear of elevators would decrease if you were able to control when the doors open and close?

Control the doors? Like... having a button that actually works to hold them open or force them open? I mean, maybe that would give me a little peace of mind right before getting in, but once they close, you're still trapped in the box, right? 

Honestly, automatic doors are just stressful in general. It reminds me of the commuter train I take sometimes to get to our secondary warehouse for training sessions. The doors on those trains are absolutely ruthless. Just last Tuesday, I saw this guy try to Indiana Jones his way through the train doors right as they were shutting. He totally didn't make it, and the doors just clamped down on his backpack. He was stuck there half in and half out for like a solid minute, and he dropped his iced coffee everywhere. It was one of those really expensive ones too, like a nitro cold brew with the sweet cream foam? I love those. I actually tried making my own cold brew at home recently because spending six bucks a day on coffee is just completely draining my bank account. I bought this fancy glass pitcher thing off Facebook Marketplace for like ten bucks. The guy who sold it to me was so strange, though. I went to his apartment to pick it up, and he had literally, I kid you not, like five massive parrots just flying free in his living room. They were squawking so loud I couldn't even hear him tell me how to clean the filter. I don't know how anyone lives with birds. The whole place just smelled like sunflower seeds and wet newspaper. 

But um... what were we talking about? Oh, the elevator doors. Right. Yeah, I don't think controlling the doors would really make a difference for me. Once I'm in there, I'm in there, and I'd still just be sweating it out until I got to my floor. I'd rather just avoid it altogether.
Do you often feel anxious or uncomfortable in situations where you have little to no control over what happens?

Control over what happens? Like, in general? I guess so, a little bit. I don't really like feeling like I'm just along for the ride. 

Actually, that reminds me of this time my buddy Mark made me go white water rafting with him for his bachelor party. Talk about zero control. You're just in this inflatable raft getting tossed around by the river, and the guide is screaming at you to paddle, but it feels like you're not even doing anything. And the water was freezing. It was up in Maine, and we went in early June, so the snow melt was still coming down the mountains. Mark thought it would be this great bonding experience for the groomsmen, but honestly, half of us were just terrified. My side of the raft hit this huge rock, and I almost fell in. If it wasn't for Mark's brother grabbing my life jacket, I would have been gone. Mark's brother is this massive guy, he plays rugby or something, and he practically lifted me back into the boat with one arm. We ended up getting completely soaked, and when we finally got back to the cabin, the hot water heater was broken. We had to take ice-cold showers after being in a freezing river all day. It was miserable. We just sat around a fire drinking cheap beer and trying to warm up. Mark actually ended up calling off the wedding like two months later, which was a whole other disaster. 

But anyway, what did you ask? Situations where I don't have control? Yeah, I'm not a fan. I definitely get a little anxious when I can't steer the ship, so to speak.
Do you think your anxiety about elevators is related to other times when you feel like you're not in control of what's happening?

Is it related to other times? Um... I don't know. Maybe? Like, I guess they both involve not being in control, but I wouldn't say they feel exactly the same. 

Like, when I'm in an elevator, it's just this very specific dread about the box itself. But feeling out of control in other things... that just makes me think of my job right now. I'm a training and development specialist for this logistics company, and they just rolled out this entirely new software system for the warehouse guys. And they didn't even consult me before they bought it. They just dumped the manuals on my desk and were like, "Okay, train three hundred people on this by Friday." It's a complete nightmare. The interface looks like it was designed in 1995, and half the time it crashes when you try to input a tracking number. I was trying to run a session yesterday, and the projector bulb blew out right in the middle of my presentation. I had to call maintenance, and this guy took forty-five minutes to bring a ladder. Meanwhile, I've got twenty forklift drivers just sitting there staring at me, and I have zero control over the situation. I tried to just talk through the rest of the slides, but nobody was paying attention. They were all just looking at their phones or talking about the game on Sunday. Did you watch the game? That final play was insane. I can't believe they went for it on fourth down instead of just kicking the field goal. My buddy lost like two hundred bucks on that play. 

But um, yeah, elevators. I don't really know if it's connected to all that other stuff. I just know I don't like getting in them.
Do you think your fear of elevators is part of a larger pattern of anxiety about situations where you feel you have no control?

A larger pattern? I mean, I guess I just said I don't like feeling out of control, but... I don't know if I'd call it a pattern. It's just elevators that really get to me. 

Speaking of patterns, though, my mom is obsessed with them. Like, she knits these crazy intricate sweaters with all these wild geometric patterns. She tried to teach me once when I was like twelve because I was grounded for a month and had nothing else to do. I got caught shooting bottle rockets off the roof of our garage with my neighbor, Kevin. Man, Kevin was a bad influence. He ended up moving to Florida to work on a shrimp boat or something weird like that. But anyway, my mom made me sit there with these huge wooden knitting needles, and I was so bad at it. I kept dropping stitches, and the thing I made ended up looking like a lopsided sock for a giant. She still has it in a box somewhere in her attic. Her attic is terrifying, by the way. It's just full of old mannequins from when my aunt used to own a boutique in the eighties. Why would anyone keep mannequins? They look like creepy statues just staring at you in the dark. I had to go up there last Thanksgiving to get the good gravy boat, and I swear one of them moved. 

But wait, what did you ask me? A pattern of anxiety? Yeah, no, I don't think it's a whole pattern thing. It's just the elevators. I just don't like being stuck in them.
Do you think your fear of elevators is connected to a more general anxiety about being in situations where things are out of your control?

I mean, I don't really think it's some big, connected thing. Like I said, I don't love being out of control, but the elevator thing feels different. It's just the elevator. 

You know, talking about control though, I was trying to fix my car last weekend. It's this 2008 Honda Civic, and the AC just completely died. I figured I could just watch a YouTube tutorial and recharge the freon myself, save a couple hundred bucks, right? So I go to the auto parts store, and the guy behind the counter—this kid who looked like he was maybe sixteen—kept trying to upsell me on all this premium synthetic oil and new wiper blades. I'm like, "Dude, I just need the AC recharge kit." Anyway, I get home, pop the hood, and I can't even find the low-pressure port. The video made it look so easy, but my engine bay was just covered in grease and dust. I ended up accidentally snapping this plastic clip off the air filter housing, and now it rattles every time I go over forty miles an hour. I swear, they build cars these days so you can't even work on them yourself. You have to take it to a dealership and pay them just to plug a computer into it. My dad used to rebuild entire carburetors on the kitchen table when I was a kid. My mom hated it, it smelled like gasoline for days... 

But, uh, yeah. General anxiety about control? No, I wouldn't really say that. Just the elevators.
Do you experience anxiety or discomfort in other small, enclosed spaces beyond just elevators?

Other small spaces? Um, no, not really. It's pretty much just the elevators. Like, I don't care about closets or anything. 

Actually, speaking of small spaces, my buddy Chris just bought this tiny house. Like, one of those literal tiny houses on wheels? He parked it in his parents' backyard because he can't afford land around here. I went over to see it last weekend, and man, it is ridiculous. The "bedroom" is just a loft you have to climb a ladder to get to, and you can't even sit up straight in bed without hitting your head on the ceiling. He was trying to show off his composting toilet, and I'm just thinking, "Dude, you're basically living in a fancy shed." He spent like sixty grand on it, too. For that kind of money, he could have just put a down payment on a normal condo, but he's all about this minimalist lifestyle now. He threw away all his video games and only owns, like, three shirts. It's wild. We used to play Call of Duty for like six hours straight on Saturdays, and now he just wants to talk about sustainable living and rainwater collection. 

But, uh, no. Closets, tiny houses, whatever... they don't bother me. Just elevators.
Do you think your fear of elevators is part of a larger issue with feeling anxious in situations where you're not in control?

I mean, you keep asking that, but no, I really don't think it's a bigger control thing. It's honestly just the elevators. I don't freak out about other stuff where I'm not in charge. 

Like, I fly all the time for work—I'm a training specialist, so they send me to different corporate branches to run onboarding sessions. And when you're on a plane, you have zero control, right? You're just sitting in a metal tube miles up in the air, trusting some pilot you've never met. But I love flying. I always get a ginger ale and just watch movies. Last time I flew to Dallas, I sat next to this guy who brought his own entire rotisserie chicken in a Tupperware container. Just pulled it out mid-flight and started eating it with his bare hands. The smell was insane. The flight attendant kept giving him these looks, but he didn't even care. He offered me a wing, which was nice of him, I guess, but I passed. I don't know how you even get a whole chicken through TSA. I had to throw away a brand new bottle of contact solution once because it was four ounces instead of three, but this guy gets a whole bird through? Makes no sense. 

But yeah, anyway, planes are fine. I don't mind not being in control there. It's literally just elevators that freak me out.

patient.answer:
Hi, yeah, thanks. So, I'm mostly here because I’ve started planning my whole day around, well, not using elevators. It’s getting a bit out of hand. Like, I’m taking five flights of stairs at my apartment every single day. Which, honestly, my calves are getting pretty strong from it, and I used to run track in high school so I don't mind the exercise, but it's exhausting when I'm carrying groceries, you know? 

But the real issue is how it's messing with my job. I'm a training specialist, I do a lot of tech and development stuff, and I actually just had to turn down leading this really cool workshop just because it was in a high-rise. The workshop was on this new scheduling software that I actually helped beta test, which was a huge deal for me because I mostly taught myself everything after I graduated, but I just couldn't do the building. 

And... I even had to stop doing house visits with one of my older computer students. His name is Arthur, really nice guy, he's just trying to learn how to video call his grandkids out in Arizona. I've never been to Arizona, but I hear the heat is a dry heat, so maybe it's not too bad compared to here? But anyway, Arthur's building doesn’t really have another option besides the elevator, like the stairs are locked or something, so I just had to stop seeing him. I just can't do the elevator thing, and it's starting to get in the way.

doctor.intent: determine if the patient's elevator avoidance is due to a specific fear
doctor.question: What is it about elevators that makes you want to avoid them?

target_item.name: Specific_Phobic_Fear
target_item.manifestation: I know an elevator in an office block is probably safe, but when I look at those old doors in my apartment building or at work, my mind treats it like I’m about to get trapped or dropped, even though part of me knows that sounds over the top.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the nature of the fear/anxiety regarding elevators (what makes the patient want to avoid them), which corresponds to the specific phobic fear where the patient explains their disproportionate fear of getting trapped or dropped.

patient.answer:
Well, it's... I mean, I know an elevator in an office block is probably safe, right? Like, they have to pass inspections and stuff. I actually read this article once about elevator inspectors, and it's wild how much they have to check. They look at the cables and the brakes—which, apparently, modern elevators have these crazy safety brakes that make it almost impossible for them to free-fall. 

But, like, when I look at those old doors in my apartment building, or even the ones at work, my mind just... it treats it like I’m about to get trapped in there. Or dropped. Even though part of me knows that sounds completely over the top, especially after reading about the brakes. It's just this overwhelming feeling. Kind of like when I tried to ride that drop tower at the state fair a few years ago. Have you ever been to the state fair? The fried Oreos are amazing, but that ride was a huge mistake. I thought I was going to die. I guess looking at an elevator gives me that exact same feeling, even if I'm just standing in the lobby holding a bag of groceries.

For that kind of money, he could have just put a down payment on a normal condo, but he's all about this minimalist lifestyle now. He threw away all his video games and only owns, like, three shirts. It's wild. We used to play Call of Duty for like six hours straight on Saturdays, and now he just wants to talk about sustainable living and rainwater collection. 

But, uh, no. Closets, tiny houses, whatever... they don't bother me. Just elevators.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's fear is specific to elevators or part of a broader anxiety issue related to loss of control
doctor.question: Do you think your fear of elevators is part of a larger issue with feeling anxious in situations where you're not in control?

target_item.reason: The doctor is repeatedly asking if the fear of elevators is related to a broader anxiety about losing control (which relates to panic disorder or agoraphobia concepts), which is not covered in the patient's specific phobia profile.

patient.answer:
I mean, you keep asking that, but no, I really don't think it's a bigger control thing. It's honestly just the elevators. I don't freak out about other stuff where I'm not in charge. 

Like, I fly all the time for work—I'm a training specialist, so they send me to different corporate branches to run onboarding sessions. And when you're on a plane, you have zero control, right? You're just sitting in a metal tube miles up in the air, trusting some pilot you've never met. But I love flying. I always get a ginger ale and just watch movies. Last time I flew to Dallas, I sat next to this guy who brought his own entire rotisserie chicken in a Tupperware container. Just pulled it out mid-flight and started eating it with his bare hands. The smell was insane. The flight attendant kept giving him these looks, but he didn't even care. He offered me a wing, which was nice of him, I guess, but I passed. I don't know how you even get a whole chicken through TSA. I had to throw away a brand new bottle of contact solution once because it was four ounces instead of three, but this guy gets a whole bird through? Makes no sense. 

But yeah, anyway, planes are fine. I don't mind not being in control there. It's literally just elevators that freak me out.
